content: Pityriasis alba is a frequently observed dermatological condition, predominantly affecting children. It is characterized by the presence of dry, fine-scaled, pale patches, most commonly on the face. The condition is self-limiting and typically requires only the application of moisturizers for management. The term pityriasis refers to the fine, scaly appearance of the lesions, while alba, derived from Latin, denotes the pale coloration of the patches. However, it is important to note that these patches are not completely depigmented. The exact cause of pityriasis alba remains unknown. However, it is hypothesized that any inflammatory process affecting the skin, such as dermatitis, may heal with residual hypopigmentation. Additionally, the overuse of corticosteroid creams, often employed in the treatment of eczema, may contribute to the development of this condition. The hypopigmentation observed in pityriasis alba is attributed to reduced melanocyte activity, resulting in fewer and smaller melanosomes. The condition is most commonly seen in children aged 3 to 16 years and is more prevalent in males than females. While it may occur more frequently in individuals with lighter skin tones, it is more noticeable in those with darker complexions. Epidemiological studies suggest that up to one-third of school-aged children in the United States may experience this condition at some point. Prevalence rates vary globally, with higher rates observed in populations with lower socioeconomic status. The clinical presentation of pityriasis alba is influenced by seasonal variations. During winter, the dry, scaly patches become more prominent due to the low humidity levels in indoor environments. In summer, the surrounding normal skin may tan, making the pale patches more conspicuous. The patches typically measure 0.5 to 2 cm in diameter but can be larger, up to 4 cm, when located on the body. The number of patches can range from 4 or 5 to over 20. These lesions are dry and exhibit very fine scaling. While they most commonly appear on the face, particularly the cheeks, approximately 20% of cases also involve the upper arms, neck, or shoulders. Diagnosis of pityriasis alba is primarily clinical, based on the characteristic appearance of the lesions during physical examination. Treatment is generally not required, as the condition resolves spontaneously over time. However, if redness, scaling, or itching is present, these symptoms can be managed with simple emollients. In some cases, hydrocortisone, a mild corticosteroid, may be used. Since the patches do not typically darken with sun exposure, effective sun protection is recommended to minimize the contrast between the hypopigmented patches and the surrounding normal skin. Cosmetic camouflage may be employed for aesthetic purposes. Tacrolimus has been reported to accelerate the resolution of the condition. In exceptionally severe cases, PUVA (psoralen and ultraviolet A) therapy may be considered. The prognosis for pityriasis alba is generally favorable. The duration of the patches can range from one month to ten years, with facial lesions commonly persisting for a year or longer.
